opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people have the intuition that proprietary data becomes more valuable as models get better, and I'd actually push back on that a bit. If you go back a few years, the conventional wisdom was that every company was sitting on a data moat. You had all this customer data, all these internal documents, and the idea was that you'd fine-tune a model on it and get something nobody else could replicate.

What we've seen instead is that the general-purpose models keep getting so much better that, for a lot of tasks, the base model plus a little bit of context just beats the specialized model you trained on your own data. The frontier keeps moving, and if you spent six months building a custom model, by the time you're done there's a new general model that's better out of the box.

So where does proprietary data still matter? I'd put it in a couple of buckets. One is data that's genuinely about your specific situation: your customers, your inventory, your codebase, your internal processes. The model can't know that from pretraining, so you need to give it to the model, but mostly through retrieval and context rather than training. That data is valuable, but it's valuable the way it always was. It's operational data, not a moat in the model sense.

The second bucket, which I think is more interesting, is data that captures how an expert actually does a task, especially the reasoning and the feedback loop, not just the end result. As models get more capable and we move toward agents doing long-horizon work, what's scarce isn't facts, it's signal about what good looks like. Can you tell whether the agent did the job well? Do you have the evaluations, the outcomes, the traces of real work? That kind of data, the kind you can turn into a reward signal, I think becomes more valuable over time.

So my advice to companies would be: don't assume your pile of documents is a moat. Ask whether you have something that lets you measure and improve performance on a task that matters to you. That's where the leverage is going.

r001.rationale: The response says increasingly capable general-purpose models can outperform specialized models trained on a company’s data, often with only a little context.

r002.rationale: It describes expert reasoning, feedback, evaluations, and traces of real work as valuable data, but does not frame skill-training data as embodied human labor.

r003.rationale: It says general models can outperform custom models, but does not claim they can reproduce proprietary training data by doing the work that generated it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually more subtle than people assume. The common view is that as models get more capable, your proprietary data becomes your moat, because the model itself is commoditized and the data is the thing nobody else has. I'd push back on part of that.

The first thing to notice is that a lot of what people call proprietary data is really just a record of how their business operated, and a sufficiently capable model doesn't need that record to be useful. If you have a decade of customer support transcripts, the model that's good at reasoning about customer problems doesn't need to be trained on your transcripts. It needs to see the one ticket in front of it, maybe your documentation, and it can do a very good job. So the value of data as training material, for most companies, goes down, not up. The frontier models are already better than what you'd get by fine-tuning on your own corpus, and that gap will keep widening.

Where data does get more valuable is in a different role. It's context, not training. The question becomes: what does the model need to know at the moment it's acting that it can't infer or look up? That's your inventory, your pricing, your contracts, the specific state of your customer relationship. That kind of data was always valuable, but it used to be trapped in systems where only a human could pull it together. Now an agent can actually consume all of it at once, which means the marginal piece of structured, accurate, current data is worth more than it was.

And then there's the data that's genuinely hard to acquire. If you're the only one who has measurements from physical processes, or outcomes that take years to observe, or interactions that only happen on your platform, that data stays scarce no matter how smart the model is. The model can reason beautifully, but it can't know things that were never recorded anywhere. So I'd say the value concentrates. Most proprietary data becomes less important, and a small slice becomes much more important.

The practical implication for a company is to stop thinking "we have a lot of data, therefore we have a moat," and start asking which data a capable model would actually be bottlenecked without. That's usually a much shorter list than people hope, and the real work is making that list clean and accessible rather than hoarding the rest.

r001.rationale: The response says capable frontier models can outperform fine-tuning on a company’s own corpus, so training on proprietary data offers less advantage as general model capability improves.

r002.rationale: It describes proprietary data as a record of business operations, but does not frame skill-training data as embodied human labor.

r003.rationale: It argues a capable model often does not need proprietary training data, but does not say the AI can recreate that data by performing the work that produced it.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what makes the data proprietary and useful. There’s a lot of information that’s valuable today because it’s hard to assemble or interpret. As models get better at doing those things, that information may become less of an advantage. If a model can infer the answer from publicly available information, owning a particular dataset doesn’t buy you as much.

But there’s another kind of data that captures something the model couldn’t otherwise know: what your customers actually want, what happened when you took a particular action, what worked and what didn’t. More capable AI can make that data more valuable, because you can do more with it.

So I’d focus less on the size of the dataset and more on the process that generates it. Do you have a product people use, where you learn something unique from those interactions and can use that learning to improve the product? That feedback loop seems like a much more durable advantage than just having a pile of data sitting somewhere.

r001.rationale: It says better models may reduce the advantage of information that is hard to assemble or infer, but does not argue that gains in general AI intelligence can outweigh training on proprietary domain data.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe skill-training data as embodied human labor.

r003.rationale: It says models may infer answers from public information, but does not argue that AI can replicate proprietary skill-training data by doing the work that produced it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on why the data is proprietary. If it’s valuable because it’s expensive to collect or organize, AI may make it much cheaper for someone else to recreate. So having a large dataset doesn’t automatically give you a durable advantage.

But if the data comes from something unique your business does—interactions with customers, experiments you run, outcomes you observe—that can become more valuable. A more capable model can make better use of that information.

So I’d focus less on the stockpile of data and more on the process that generates it. Do you have a product that lets you learn something nobody else can learn, and can you use that learning to make the product better? That feedback loop seems much more defensible than simply having a database that other people don’t have.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may make costly-to-collect data easier to recreate, but does not compare general AI intelligence gains with the advantage of training on proprietary domain data.

r002.rationale: It does not describe proprietary skill-training data as embodied human labor.

r003.rationale: It says AI may help others recreate expensive data, but does not say AI can reproduce skill-training data by doing the work that originally generated it.
